routes.description: Defend Jesus's earthly historicity through Paul's beliefs, identifying kinship language, and later testimony about a traceable family and movement.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the cited evidence is better explained by a recently deceased earthly person than by a wholly celestial Christ later historicized.

motionBridge.description: The earliest Christian evidence supports an earthly historical Jesus.

centralBridges.description: Paul understood Jesus's death, burial, birth, and identity as earthly realities.
James was identified as Jesus's biological brother rather than merely a fellow believer.
Traditions about Jesus's relatives preserve a real and traceable family line.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Ancient naming conventions used relational descriptions to distinguish specific people.
Non-Pauline writers supply information independent enough to support historicity.

routes.description: Challenge historicity by showing that Paul's evidence is celestial or ambiguous and that later narratives lack demonstrably independent, reliable sourcing.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the surviving evidence does not favor an earthly founder over a celestial Christ revealed through scripture and later placed in narrative history.

motionBridge.description: Early Christian belief can be explained without an earthly historical Jesus.

centralBridges.description: Paul locates knowledge of Jesus in scripture and revelation rather than earthly testimony.
Paul's brother terminology does not securely identify a biological relative of Jesus.
Later family and Roman testimony lacks sufficiently early independent sourcing.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Paul's birth language occurs within an allegorical argument and remains historically ambiguous.
Acts conflicts with Paul's autobiographical statements and cannot securely fill historical gaps.

sections.title: Paul's earthly or celestial Jesus
sections.rationale: Paul is the earliest central evidence, and whether his death, burial, and revelation language locates Jesus on earth directly affects the motion.

sections.title: James and brother terminology
sections.rationale: The interpretation of James as a biological or cultic brother is a direct potential link between Paul and an earthly Jesus.

sections.title: Later family and external traditions
sections.rationale: Hegesippus and related traditions could corroborate a historical family, but their date, transmission, and sourcing are heavily contested.

sections.title: Burial, Acts, and Paul's biography
sections.rationale: The earthly-burial inference and Acts-based account of Paul's background materially test whether the pro route survives the celestial alternative.

moves.speaker: Stephen Boyce
moves.proposition: Paul continued to understand Jesus as a physical person who died, was buried, and was crucified even after Paul's conversion.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Jesus, that's not the point of this debate. Regardless of that conversion from a Pharisee on the Sanhedrin to a Christian, he continued to recognize in first Corinthians that Jesus died and that his physical body was actually buried.

moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gave Boyce the opening floor, and this uninterrupted span remains within that opening statement.

response.rationale: This is an opening constructive claim advancing the pro route before any selected opposing move appears, so it has no permissible earlier target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim about Paul's post-conversion belief is recoverable and bounded, though the inferential limits of death and burial language remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cited Pauline language supports Boyce's reading, but the move treats physical-earthly location as firmer than the quoted terms alone establish.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from death, bodily burial, and crucifixion to a physical Jesus is coherent, with earthly location left as one implicit bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific Pauline claims are invoked, but the span does not quote or defend their textual context against a celestial interpretation.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive opening, it clearly advances an adopted central burden without needing to answer an earlier selected move.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially advances the central bridge that Paul understood Jesus as an earthly physical person.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move does not yet represent or attack a selected live alternative, so charity is not tested.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span relies on Boyce's reading of Pauline death, burial, and crucifixion language as evidence of physical existence.

moves.speaker: Stephen Boyce
moves.proposition: Paul's description of James as the Lord's brother follows ancient identifying practice and therefore indicates a specific biological relative.

sourceSpan.excerpt: premise two description family connections and locations were necessities to identify people of interest accurately. Paul identified James as a legal brother not a potential general brother in order to not confuse his audience with James the brother of John.

moves.attributionBasis: This span is part of Boyce's uninterrupted opening and explicitly labels his second premise before the moderator changes speakers.

response.rationale: The move constructively establishes the pro kinship route before any selected con response, so no earlier selected target is available or required.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is clear, but the phrase legal brother is not adequately distinguished from biological brother and alternative usages are not qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Naming conventions support specificity, but they do not by themselves establish that the relationship specified must be biological rather than cultic.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The identifying-convention inference is intelligible, but specificity does not alone entail the biological sense asserted in the conclusion.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move invokes comparative naming practice, yet its decisive bridge from identification to biological kinship remains materially underdefended.

responsiveness.rationale: As an opening constructive, it directly states and supports the selected kinship burden without an earlier response obligation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: If sustained, identifying James as a biological brother would strongly advance a central historicity bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: No selected opposing alternative has yet appeared, so representational charity is not tested.

moves.evidenceBasis: The stated evidence is a pattern of relational descriptions used to distinguish people who shared common names in ancient texts.

moves.speaker: Stephen Boyce
moves.proposition: Hegesippus preserves a continuing dynasty of Jesus's relatives in Jerusalem, supporting the conclusion that Jesus was a real man with traceable family.

sourceSpan.excerpt: So my premise three is this. The family, the dynasty, this dynasty of Jesus continued as leaders within the church of Jerusalem until about the time 110 AD. Therefore, Jesus was a real man who had real relatives that could be traced.

moves.attributionBasis: Boyce explicitly announces his third premise during his uninterrupted opening statement and draws its stated historicity conclusion in the same span.

response.rationale: This is a constructive presentation of the later-family bridge and occurs before the selected con challenge to that evidence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion and time scope are recoverable, but dynasty shifts between relatives, leaders, and descendants without a stable genealogical definition.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical conclusion exceeds what a later transmitted family tradition can establish without source, transmission, and legendary-development qualifications.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A genuine traceable family would support historicity, but the inference assumes the later dynasty report reliably preserves first-century genealogy.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The evidence is relevant but late and mediated, while this span supplies no independent corroboration or source-critical defense.

responsiveness.rationale: The move clearly opens and advances the selected later-family issue without an earlier selected response target.

relevanceBurden.rationale: A reliable continuing family line would materially support the central pro bridge, though it is not by itself the complete motion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The constructive does not represent a selected opposing account, leaving charity untested.

moves.evidenceBasis: The move relies on a reported Hegesippan tradition about relatives and successive Jerusalem leadership extending into the second century.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: Paul's death, burial, and resurrection language does not locate Jesus on earth because Paul presents scripture and revelation as his sources.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Jesus is made of Jewish flesh, Davidic flesh in fact, and believes that he became immortal and died and was crucified and was resurrected. The question is where. Paul never places any of these things on earth. He says the crucifixion and the burial are known from scripture.

moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly transferred the floor to Carrier, and this continuous passage occurs within Carrier's opening response to Boyce.

components.text: Paul believed Jesus died, was physically buried, and was crucified.
Those descriptions establish an earthly physical person rather than a celestial event.

response.rationale: Carrier concedes the death and burial predicates, then directly disputes the decisive earthly-location inference by supplying scripture and revelation as the alternative source framework.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes conceding Paul's predicates from contesting their location and explicitly identifies the limited scope of the disagreement.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The source-language point supports ambiguity and a celestial reading, though saying Paul never places any event on earth requires broader textual defense.

charity.alternative: Boyce argues that Paul's references to death, physical burial, and crucifixion indicate an earthly physical Jesus.
charity.decisiveQualification: Carrier preserves Boyce's claimed predicates and disputes where Paul locates the events rather than denying that Paul affirmed them.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The concession-and-distinction structure is coherent and directly isolates the missing bridge from burial language to earthly location.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Multiple Pauline source categories are identified, but the universal claim about earthly placement is summarized rather than demonstrated passage by passage.

responsiveness.rationale: The move explicitly contacts both the textual premise and the decisive earthly-location inference in the strongest selected pro target.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central pro bridge concerning Paul's understanding of Jesus as an earthly person.

representationalCharity.rationale: Carrier accurately concedes Boyce's strongest textual predicates before challenging only their claimed earthly implication.

moves.evidenceBasis: Carrier relies on Paul's attribution of knowledge to scripture and revelation and the alleged absence of explicit earthly placement.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: Galatians identifies James because Paul's argument requires disclosure of everyone he met, while the grammar leaves biological and cultic brotherhood ambiguous.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Dr. Boyce brings up a new argument, which is the proposal that we can only explain why Paul names James this way if he meant a biological brother of Jesus. That actually takes the argument out of context. He's a brother of the Lord, could mean a biological brother, could mean a baptized Christian.

moves.attributionBasis: Carrier names Boyce's argument directly in his uninterrupted opening and supplies his grammatical and contextual reply within the same speaking turn.

components.text: The relational description was used to identify a specific James.
Identification as the Lord's brother establishes biological rather than cultic kinship.

response.rationale: Carrier answers the identifying-purpose claim with Paul's disclosure context and directly contests the decisive biological inference by preserving two live meanings of brother.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes why James is named from what brother means and expressly preserves both biological and baptized-Christian readings.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Carrier argues for ambiguity rather than categorical fictive kinship, matching the limited force of the grammatical and contextual warrant supplied.

charity.alternative: Boyce argues that naming practice makes James a specifically identified biological brother of Jesus.
charity.decisiveQualification: Carrier recognizes that Boyce's argument concerns the explanatory function of the attached description, not merely the broad semantic range of brother.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move supplies a clear alternative explanation for naming James and separates identification from biological relationship without contradiction.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The immediate argumentative context and grammatical distinction provide strong support, though the scholarly grammar claim remains compressed.

responsiveness.rationale: Both the naming-convention premise and its decisive biological conclusion receive explicit, issue-specific answers.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the central pro bridge linking James biologically to Jesus.

representationalCharity.rationale: Carrier accurately frames Boyce's novel explanatory argument, though the excerpt compresses some of Boyce's comparative naming evidence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The move relies on Galatians' disclosure context, the exclusionary grammatical reading, and the acknowledged semantic range of brother terminology.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: Hegesippus is too late, legendary, and unsourced to establish that traditions about Jesus's family preserve genuine first-century history.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Hegesippus, this is late second century, 180 to 200 AD. The quotations we have from him are full of really absurd apocrypha, ridiculous legends and stories. We're looking at 150 years after the fact where legends had grown up about the family of Jesus.

moves.attributionBasis: This passage occurs in Carrier's uninterrupted opening and explicitly addresses Boyce's Hegesippus evidence by name and date.

components.text: Hegesippus reports a continuing dynasty of Jesus's relatives and Jerusalem leaders.
That report reliably preserves a traceable family line from the first century.
The reported succession specifically substantiates the claimed endpoint around 110.

response.rationale: Carrier directly attacks the decisive reliability bridge through lateness and legendary content, but does not separately analyze Boyce's specific succession chronology and endpoint.

precisionFindings.rationale: The source-critical objection is recoverable and temporally bounded, although the standards for labeling the traditions apocryphal remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Lateness and legendary features justify skepticism, but the categorical dismissal relies heavily on asserted implausibility without demonstrating each relevant tradition's derivation.

charity.alternative: Boyce treats Hegesippus's family succession as evidence that Jesus had traceable real relatives.
charity.decisiveQualification: The pro claim relies on the family tradition's historical transmission, not merely on Hegesippus being an early author.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from late legendary transmission to reduced historical value is coherent, though it does not by itself prove total fabrication.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Date and legendary-development concerns are relevant, but the span asserts rather than demonstrates the specific source failures of the family tradition.

responsiveness.rationale: The decisive reliability component is contacted directly, while the particular succession structure and proposed endpoint remain untreated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially attacks the central pro bridge that later family traditions preserve real genealogy.

representationalCharity.rationale: Carrier fairly identifies the family-line claim and its late source, with some rhetorical compression of Boyce's transmission defense.

moves.evidenceBasis: Carrier invokes the late date, legendary character, and lack of early corroboration for the surviving Hegesippan family traditions.

moves.speaker: Stephen Boyce
moves.proposition: Paul's reference to physical burial supplies an earthly element, while Paul's proximity to the earliest persecution makes ignorance of an executed man implausible.

sourceSpan.excerpt: when we go back to 1 Corinthians 15 he uses this defense, mention of not only that he died but that he was physically buried. There was some sort of burial for him that indicates something we do here on earth, not something up in outer space.

moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gave Boyce this rebuttal period, and the span answers Carrier's celestial-location argument in a continuous Boyce turn.

components.text: Paul affirms an actual death, burial, crucifixion, and resurrection.
Paul never locates those events on earth and derives them from scripture or revelation.
Celestial cosmology supplies a coherent alternative location for burial.

response.rationale: Boyce directly argues that burial implies earth, contacting Carrier's decisive location challenge, but does not answer Carrier's broader source claim or developed celestial-burial alternative.

precisionFindings.rationale: The earthly-burial inference is clearly recoverable, but its dependence on ordinary modern burial assumptions rather than the disputed cosmology is implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Ordinary burial favors an earthly reading, but the move does not yet engage the period-specific celestial-copy framework used by the opposing account.

charity.alternative: Carrier accepts an actual burial but argues that Paul never places it on earth and knows it through scripture.
charity.decisiveQualification: Carrier's position does not deny that Paul believed in burial; it disputes the burial's location and evidential source.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The ordinary inference from physical burial to earth is intelligible, but it leaves Carrier's alternative cosmological bridge unresolved.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: First Corinthians burial language is directly relevant, yet the move supplies little contextual support for the specifically earthly location asserted.

responsiveness.rationale: The decisive earthly-location issue is contacted, but the scripture-revelation basis and celestial-burial model are not fully answered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the central con claim that Paul's Jesus can remain celestial despite death and burial.

representationalCharity.rationale: Boyce accurately frames the dispute as earthly versus outer-space burial rather than claiming Carrier denies Paul's burial language.

moves.evidenceBasis: The move relies on First Corinthians 15's burial statement and the ordinary association of physical burial with earthly practice.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: Acts cannot establish Paul's Jerusalem activity because it conflicts with Paul's own statement that Judean churches did not know him before his conversion.

sourceSpan.excerpt: The fact that Acts claims that Paul was there for the execution of Stephen, that doesn't tell us what Paul or Stephen were saying or believing at the time. Paul says himself in Galatians 1 that no one in Judea knew him until long after he converted.

moves.attributionBasis: The moderator transferred the rebuttal floor to Carrier, who explicitly answers Boyce's Acts-based Paul chronology in this uninterrupted span.

components.text: Physical burial supplies an earthly location for Jesus's death narrative.
Acts places Paul near Stephen's execution and the earliest Jerusalem controversy.
Paul's proximity makes ignorance of a recently executed earthly Jesus implausible.

response.rationale: Carrier directly contests the Acts-based proximity premise and its autobiographical warrant, but this selected span does not answer Boyce's separate burial-location inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The Acts-Paul conflict is clearly stated and bounded to pre-conversion Judean recognition, though unknown personally and unknown by reputation remain compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Galatians creates a serious tension with Acts, but the categorical claim that Paul's statement disproves all Jerusalem presence requires a stronger semantic argument.

charity.alternative: Boyce uses Acts to place Paul at Stephen's execution and near the earliest dispute about Jesus.
charity.decisiveQualification: Boyce's proximity argument depends on Acts being historically usable and on the controversy concerning an earthly executed man.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Contrasting Acts with Paul's earlier autobiographical evidence is coherent, though the inference from churches not knowing Paul to no Jerusalem presence is disputable.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The appeal to Paul's own letter over Acts is evidentially appropriate, but the exact scope of the apparent contradiction remains compressed.

responsiveness.rationale: The move addresses the Acts-based proximity argument and its consequence but leaves the selected burial-location component unanswered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It advances a necessary subsidiary bridge concerning Acts' reliability rather than directly resolving the complete celestial-origin motion.

representationalCharity.rationale: Carrier accurately identifies Boyce's reliance on Acts and answers its historical use without imputing a stronger theological claim.

moves.evidenceBasis: The move compares Acts' Stephen narrative with Paul's autobiographical statement about being unknown to Judean churches before later contact.
